newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Leaders beat drum of confidence in HK's future.
newsitem.headline: Leaders beat drum of confidence in HK's future.

text.p: Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting Tung Chee-hwa defended his plans to tighten civil liberties laws and painted a bright picture of Hong Kong after the handover to China in talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday.

Tung's upbeat message of confidence was reinforced from Beijing when Chinese President Jiang Zemin appeared on Cable News Network (CNN) with fresh assurances for Hong Kong when it becomes a Chinese Special Administrative Region on July 1.
Tung has sparked angry opposition at home and abroad for his plans to roll back civil liberties when more than 10 years of British rule ends.
His proposals include requiring demonstrators to obtain police permits for protests and prohibiting foreign funding for local political parties.

The former shipping magnate, who is preparing to step into shoes of Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten in 53 days, argues the changes are no stricter than those in developed nations and are needed to preserve stability in sensitive transitional times.
Kohl told reporters after the meeting he was confident that China would stick to its treaty obligations to maintain Hong Kong's separate freedoms and capitalist way of life intact.

The pledges were codified in the 1984 Sino-British treaty on the transition and spelled out in the Basic Law, the constitution for post-colonial Hong Kong which guarantees that Hong Kong people and not Chinese officials will govern the territory.
Jiang told CNN that no Chinese leader, including himself, would be above the law in Hong Kong.
"I wish to emphasise that in the administration of Hong Kong, no matter how powerful I am, I will act according to the Basic Law of Hong Kong's Special Administrative Region," Jiang said.

Tung, who was selected for the post in December by a China-appointed panel and is still grappling with his new political role, has hit out at his opponents for painting a gloomy picture about Hong Kong and ignoring business confidence.
Pro-democracy legislators, lawyers and human rights activists have carried their battle against the proposed changes to foreign capitals.

They have also slammed as unconstitutional China's plan to install an interim provisional legislature in place of an elected chamber returned in 1995 under reforms spearheaded by Patten to China's fury.

Martin Lee, leader of the populist Democratic Party who will lose his seat when the elected legislature is dissolved, recently staged an exhaustive lobbying trip to Europe and the United States which culminated in a meeting with President Clinton.
Tung lashed out at Lee for "badmouthing" Hong Kong abroad but cancelled his own tentative plans to visit North America due to pressure of work.
Lee said he was disappointed he did not get to meet Kohl to express his fears of Hong Kong's freedoms being eroded.
Kohl, who flew in from New Zealand on Friday morning, was scheduled to depart on Saturday.

"He met the Hong Kong governor and future chief executive Mr Tung and neither of them was elected by Hong Kong people," Lee told reporters after a meeting with German members of parliament accompanying Kohl on his trip.

"I told them about, principally about, my concerns about the laws of some of our freedoms when we are going to have this appointed legislature and it's already beginning to pass laws, rolling back human rights protection laws, and that the rule of law is not the same again because the legislature is not democratically elected by the people."

The chancellor met Patten for one-and-a-half hours of talks before embarking on a two-hour Chinese lunch and a shopping trip in Hong Kong's antiques quarter, to the astonishment of passers-by including a group of German tourists.

The provisional legislature is due to meet in the Chinese border town of Shenzhen on Saturday to discuss the outcome of a three-week consultation exercise that sought the views of Hong Kong people on Tung's proposed changes.
A key Tung aide said earlier this week he expected some of the proposed changes to be softened slightly but not abandoned altogether.
